analysis: The closest option develops philosophy of belief and ethics, comparative narratives, cultural heritage, historical method and social context. World Myth and Literature, heritage study and philosophical argument overlap with ways of interpreting beliefs, texts and cultural practices. Sociology, law, psychology and politics add explanations of institutions and collective life without becoming theological study.

The second option draws on ethical argument, AI and human rights, with cellular science, disease and genetics supplying grounds for assessing claims about interventions. Sustainability gateways, climate science, governance, lifecycle analysis and renewable design provide a sustained environmental strand. Climate Change is a better fit than taking an applied sustainability research project in term one. Its climate justice and stakeholder work connect environmental knowledge to responsibility.

Biblical languages and confessional theology need a sequence of original-language acquisition, scriptural interpretation and specialist theological study. Literature, mythology, philosophy and heritage have bounded contributions but no sustained substitute. A spiritual care or ministry direction lacks applied theology and specialist care or formation. The reason is academic substance. The two retained courses of study satisfy scheduling and distinctness.

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics

GOSPHIL214.name: Philosophy of Mind

GOSPHIL311.name: Philosophy of Emotion

GOSPHIL313.name: Free Will, Time & the Self
GOSPHIL313.contribution: examines free will, time, luck and the self as philosophical questions about agency, responsibility and human existence

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.contribution: provides concepts of authority, liberty, pluralism, justice and political obligation for analysing religious and political coexistence

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.contribution: studies ideological conflict, radicalisation, violence, reconciliation and peacebuilding

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.contribution: introduces sociological theories of institutions, inequality and collective life for analysing religious communities and social change

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.contribution: teaches qualitative design, interpretation and reflexivity for investigating lived meanings and communities

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.contribution: studies civil society, solidarity, social trust, public spheres and migrant inclusion

HCBBIOM311.name: Pharmacology
HCBBIOM311.contribution: studies drug actions, toxicity and therapeutic consequences as evidence for health-intervention ethics

HCBBIOM313.name: Mechanisms of Disease
HCBBIOM313.contribution: Integrates anatomy and physiology to explain disease mechanisms, symptoms, diagnostic findings and treatment reasoning.

HCBGATE101.name: Foundation of Life, Health & Biomedicine
HCBGATE101.contribution: establishes cellular, molecular, genetic and physiological foundations for evaluating ethical questions about genetic intervention and human life

HCBLIFE211.name: Molecular Cell Biology
HCBLIFE211.contribution: examines molecular and cellular mechanisms and research reproducibility relevant to biotechnology and genetic intervention

HCBLIFE212.name: Human Physiology

HCBLIFE213.name: Biochemistry
HCBLIFE213.contribution: Uses enzymes, biomolecules and metabolic pathways to explain biological mechanisms and connect them to disease.

HCBLIFE214.name: Life Science Laboratory

HCBLIFE311.name: Molecular Pathology & Genetics
HCBLIFE311.contribution: studies genetic mutations, disease, cell death, repair, testing and explicit ethical considerations

HCBPSYC111.name: Social Psychology
HCBPSYC111.contribution: examines how social influence, groups and norms shape beliefs and behaviour

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.contribution: uses material evidence to study ancient identities, craft, ritual and cultural traditions across world regions

MCCHEAM211.name: African Art & Heritage
MCCHEAM211.contribution: studies spiritual and social meaning in western-African visual traditions and their colonial and museum histories

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.contribution: studies artistic and cultural exchange between Renaissance Italy, Islamic courts and the wider Mediterranean

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.contribution: directly examines how democracy, myth and religion interacted in ancient political and cultural life

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.contribution: develops visual analysis and art-historical writing for interpreting identity, belief, heritage and meaning

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.contribution: teaches close textual interpretation and genre analysis for studying narratives about belief and human meaning without claiming scriptural exegesis

MCCLITR112.name: Great Literary Works
MCCLITR112.contribution: traces literary treatments of mortality, responsibility, community and organised religion across historical periods

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.contribution: compares mythic narratives across world traditions and their circulation through text, image, orality and performance

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.contribution: studies storytelling, race, power and systemic exclusion through critical media analysis, supplying a bounded lens on cultural representation

alignment.rationale: Both use philosophical argument to examine God, meaning and human experience. Groningen centres philosophy of religion and spirituality.
Both interpret foundational narratives and how they are retold. UCR studies myths across literary traditions. Groningen focuses on foundational religious texts.
Both develop arguments about moral responsibility and the good life. Groningen examines those questions through theological ethics.
